content: Craniopharyngiomas are the most common benign tumors affecting the hypothalamo-pituitary region in children. Over 90% of these tumors are cystic in nature. The optimal treatment strategy for cystic craniopharyngiomas remains a subject of debate. Radical surgical resection is considered the preferred treatment when the tumor is located in a favorable position. However, in cases where the tumor's location is less favorable, gross-total or partial resection followed by radiotherapy is the standard approach in adults. This approach, however, carries significant risks of morbidity, particularly in pediatric patients. Intracystic bleomycin has been explored as a treatment option to potentially delay the need for radiotherapy or radical surgery, thereby reducing associated morbidity. This review represents the second update of a previously published Cochrane review, aiming to evaluate the benefits and potential harms of intracystic bleomycin in children with cystic craniopharyngiomas. The objective of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of intracystic bleomycin in children aged 0 to 18 years with cystic craniopharyngiomas, compared to placebo (no treatment), surgical interventions (with or without radiotherapy), or other intracystic treatments. The search strategy involved a comprehensive review of electronic databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE/PubMed, and EMBASE, up to February 2016. Additional sources, such as reference lists of relevant articles, conference proceedings, and trial registries, were also examined. The inclusion criteria focused on randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized trials, or controlled clinical trials (CCTs) that compared intracystic bleomycin with other treatment modalities for cystic craniopharyngiomas in children. Two independent reviewers conducted the study selection, data extraction, and risk of bias assessment. Statistical analyses were performed using risk ratios (RR) for binary outcomes and mean differences (MD) for continuous outcomes. In cases where one treatment group experienced no events and only one study was available, Fisher's exact test was used. The analysis adhered to the guidelines outlined in the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions. The review did not identify any studies in which the sole difference between treatment groups was the use of intracystic bleomycin. One RCT comparing intracystic bleomycin with intracystic phosphorus-32 (32P) was identified, involving seven pediatric patients. No additional studies were found in this update. The included study was determined to have a high risk of bias, and survival outcomes could not be evaluated. There was no clear evidence of a difference between treatment groups in terms of cyst size reduction (MD -0.15, 95% CI -0.69 to 0.39, p = 0.59), neurological status (Fisher's exact p = 0.429), third nerve paralysis (Fisher's exact p = 1.00), fever (RR 2.92, 95% CI 0.73 to 11.70, p = 0.13), or total adverse effects (RR 1.75, 95% CI 0.68 to 4.53, p = 0.25). However, there was a significant difference favoring the 32P group for the occurrence of headache and vomiting (Fisher's exact p = 0.029 for both outcomes). The quality of evidence for all outcomes was rated as very low. In conclusion, no RCTs, quasi-randomized trials, or CCTs were identified in which intracystic bleomycin was the only variable between treatment groups. As a result, no definitive conclusions can be drawn regarding the efficacy or safety of intracystic bleomycin in children with cystic craniopharyngiomas. The single available RCT comparing intracystic bleomycin with 32P was underpowered and did not provide sufficient evidence to support the use of either agent. Based on the current evidence, no recommendations can be made for the use of intracystic bleomycin in this patient population. High-quality RCTs are urgently needed to address this gap in knowledge.
